original_question: Do the prime numbers contain infinitely many patterns of the forms {m, m + [n^c], m + 2[n^c], ..., m + ℓ[n^c]} and {m, m + [n^c1], ..., m + [n^cℓ]} for given positive real exponents c, c1, ..., cℓ?
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper’s exact target: it asks about configurations inside the prime numbers, and it includes exactly the two pattern families that appear in Problem 30, with arbitrary positive real exponents.
missing_details: The paper fixes a length parameter ℓ in N; this should be stated explicitly.
The bracket notation [x] should be defined as the integer part (floor) of x.
The quantified variables m and n should be made explicit as positive integers.
It should be stated explicitly that every element of each displayed set is required to be prime.

To stay paper-faithful, no extra assumptions should be added on the exponents: the paper only assumes c,c1,...,cℓ are positive real numbers, with no distinctness, irrationality, or nonintegrality requirement.
refined_question: Fix ℓ∈N and positive real numbers c,c1,...,cℓ, and write [x]=⌊x⌋. Do there exist infinitely many pairs of positive integers (m,n) such that every element of {m, m+[n^c], m+2[n^c], ..., m+ℓ[n^c]} is prime, and likewise infinitely many pairs of positive integers (m,n) such that every element of {m, m+[n^{c1}], ..., m+[n^{cℓ}]} is prime?
justification: The nearest official formulation is Problem 30 in Section 6.3, where Frantzikinakis explicitly asks whether the primes contain exactly these two kinds of Hardy-field-type patterns. The surrounding paragraph says this problem is motivated by trying to transfer Hardy field extensions of Szemerédi’s theorem to the primes, and the sentence immediately after the problem notes that the case of rational exponents follows from Tao–Ziegler. Your draft already captures the mathematical core, but to make it fully stand-alone and faithful to the paper one must expose the quantifiers over ℓ,m,n and define the operator [·] as integer part.
